# ktor-svelte main

> Ship a Ktor API and a SvelteKit frontend as one app: one JAR, one port, and a TypeScript client that matches your routes.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/introduction

# What is ktor-svelte?

ktor-svelte is a Gradle plugin and a Ktor plugin that turn a Ktor API and a SvelteKit frontend into one application. In production it is a single JAR on a single port. In development you open Ktor's port and get Vite's hot reload.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    transport {
        json()
    }
}
```

Write a route in Kotlin, save, and call it from Svelte with full types:

```ts
import { api } from '#api';

const note = await api.notes.create({ title: 'Buy milk' });
```

**Made with AI**
This project was made heavily with AI, and nothing is guaranteed. It has real tests, but read the code before you trust it with anything important. While the version starts with `0.`, expect breaking changes.

## How the pieces fit

```
frontend/              SvelteKit with adapter-static
src/main/kotlin/       your Ktor app with install(Svelte)
build.gradle.kts       the ktor-svelte Gradle plugin
```

1. **At build time**, the Gradle plugin installs your frontend dependencies, runs the SvelteKit build and copies the static output into the JAR, together with a manifest that lists every file and its hash.
2. **At run time**, `install(Svelte)` serves those files on the same port as your API. Your Ktor routes always win, missing pages get the SPA fallback, and hashed assets are cached forever.
3. **In development**, the plugin proxies page requests to Vite, so you get hot reload on Ktor's port with the same origin as production, and the TypeScript client is regenerated from your routes whenever the app starts.

The frontend is plain files, so there is no Node process in production. SvelteKit runs in the browser, and Ktor is the only backend. The [FAQ](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/faq) explains why ktor-svelte uses `adapter-static` and what that means for server-side rendering.

## What you get

- **One port, one JAR.** Works with `jar`, Shadow and Ktor's `buildFatJar`.
- **Your routes win.** Anything you define in Ktor beats the frontend, whatever order you register it in.
- **Generated TypeScript.** Types, services, validation rules and typed errors from your Ktor routes, with no npm dependencies.
- **Real hot reload.** One command runs Vite, the Kotlin compiler and your app.
- **Secure defaults.** CSP, security headers, origin check, body and rate limits, hidden error details.
- **Fast defaults.** Immutable caching, ETags, precompressed files, compressed API responses, real 404s for stale chunks.
- **Frontend libraries from Kotlin.** Tailwind, DaisyUI, Lucide, i18n and image optimization, configured in Gradle.
- **Any package manager.** Bun, pnpm, npm or Yarn, picked from your lockfile.
- **IntelliJ run configurations.** One click starts everything.

## Where to go next

- New project: [Getting started](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/getting-started)
- Existing Ktor or SvelteKit app: [Add to an existing project](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/existing-project)
- See it working first: [Examples](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/examples)
- Deciding between setups: [Compared with other setups](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/comparison)
- Asking an AI assistant: give it [llms-full.txt](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/llms-full.txt), the whole documentation as one Markdown file, or the index at [llms.txt](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/llms.txt)

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/comparison

# Compared with other setups

ktor-svelte is one way to put a Ktor API and a SvelteKit frontend together. This page compares it with the common alternatives, so you can tell whether it fits before you start.

## At a glance

| | ktor-svelte | SvelteKit `adapter-node` in front of Ktor | Static frontend on a CDN, Ktor API elsewhere | Ktor `staticResources` by hand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Processes in production | 1 JVM | Node and JVM | JVM, plus the CDN | 1 JVM |
| Origins | One | One, through the Node server | Two, so CORS | One |
| Server-side rendering per request | No, prerendering at build time | Yes | No | No |
| Typed client for your Ktor routes | Generated | Write or generate it yourself | Write or generate it yourself | Write or generate it yourself |
| SPA fallback, trailing slashes, stale chunk 404s | Built in | Built in | CDN rules | Write them yourself |
| Caching headers, ETags, precompressed files | Built in | Built in for assets | CDN | Partly, configure yourself |
| Dev loop | One command, hot reload on Ktor's port | Two servers, proxy config | Two servers, CORS in dev | Rebuild the frontend or run two servers |
| Deploy | One JAR | Two artifacts | Two artifacts | One JAR |

## SvelteKit with `adapter-node` in front of Ktor

SvelteKit runs as its own Node server, renders pages per request, and calls Ktor from `+page.server.ts` or forwards `/api` to it.

Pick this when you need per-request server-side rendering: pages with personal data that search engines must see, or first paint from data that changes on every request. You also get `+server.ts` endpoints and form actions.

The cost is two runtimes to deploy, monitor and scale, auth that has to work in both, and a hop between them. With ktor-svelte, prerendered pages cover content known at build time, and pages that need API data render in the browser. The [FAQ](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/faq) explains this choice in more detail.

## A static frontend on a CDN with a separate Ktor API

The frontend is built with `adapter-static` and uploaded to a CDN or object storage, and the browser calls Ktor on another domain.

Pick this when the frontend has a very high share of traffic, or a team that deploys it on its own schedule. The CDN serves files from close to the user.

The cost is two deployments that must stay compatible, CORS and its preflight requests, and cookies that need `SameSite=None` or a shared parent domain. ktor-svelte keeps one origin, so cookies and the origin check work without extra configuration. You can still put a CDN in front of the single app: hashed files under `/_app/immutable/` are marked cacheable forever.

## Ktor serving the build with `staticResources`

You copy the SvelteKit build into your resources yourself and serve it with Ktor's static content support.

This works for a small app with only a few pages. Everything ktor-svelte adds is left to you: wiring the frontend build into Gradle, the SPA fallback that does not swallow API 404s, redirects for trailing slashes, real 404s for missing chunks after a deploy, precompressed files, CSP hashes for SvelteKit's inline scripts, the dev proxy and the TypeScript client.

## Other full-stack frameworks

- **Spring Boot with a frontend build plugin** follows the same idea on Spring. ktor-svelte is the Ktor and SvelteKit version, with the generated client and dev proxy included.
- **Kotlin frontend frameworks**, such as Compose for Web or Kobweb, share one language across the stack. ktor-svelte keeps the frontend in TypeScript and Svelte, and shares types through the generated client instead.
- **JavaScript full-stack frameworks**, such as SvelteKit on its own, Next.js or Nuxt, keep everything in one JavaScript runtime. Choose ktor-svelte when the backend is, or should be, on the JVM.

## When ktor-svelte is not the right fit

- You need server-side rendering on every request.
- The frontend and the backend are deployed by different teams on different schedules.
- The app mounts under a sub-path, which ktor-svelte does not support yet.
- You want SvelteKit's `+page.server.ts`, `+server.ts` or form actions. In ktor-svelte, Ktor routes take their place.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/getting-started

# Getting started

Create a new Ktor and SvelteKit project with everything wired up, then run it.

One command asks a few questions and sets up a working project, always on the latest release. You need Java 17 or newer and one of Bun, pnpm, npm or Yarn.

**macOS and Linux:**

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/main/scripts/setup.sh | sh
```

**Windows:**

```powershell
powershell -c "irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/main/scripts/setup.ps1 | iex"
```

It asks a few questions, and you can press Enter for the defaults. Then start it:

```bash
./gradlew svelteDevAll
```

| Question | Flag | Default | What you get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project name, Kotlin package, package manager | `--name`, `--package`, `--package-manager` | `my-app`, `com.example.app`, first one found | |
| TypeScript client | `--generate-ts` | yes | `generateTs` turned on |
| DaisyUI, Tailwind, Lucide | `--daisy`, `--tailwind`, `--lucide` | yes | Configured in `build.gradle.kts` |
| i18n | `--i18n`, `--locales`, `--locale-strategy` | no | Message files and the chosen strategy |
| Sign in | `--auth` | no | Cookie sessions, hashed passwords, routes, and login and account pages |
| Postgres | `--database` | no | Exposed, HikariCP, `compose.yaml` and a small example table |
| Flyway, only with Postgres | `--flyway` | yes | Migrations in `src/main/resources/db/migration` |
| No package folders | `--idea-ext` | yes | Kotlin files directly in `src/main/kotlin`, and IntelliJ knows the package through the `idea-ext` plugin |
| Convention plugin | `--conventions` | no | `build-logic` with shared Kotlin and ktlint setup, for multi-module projects |
| Dockerfile | `--docker` | yes | A multi-stage build that runs the JAR as a non-root user |
| GitHub Actions | `--github-actions` | yes | A CI workflow with Actions pinned to commit SHAs |
| Git repository, only if git is installed | `--git` | yes | `git init` |
| Open in IntelliJ, only if it is installed | `--open-idea` | yes, but no with `--yes` | Opens the project when it is ready |

Every project also gets a Gradle version catalog, JSON and typed error responses, ktlint, ESLint and Prettier, a `README.md`, a `.env.example` and a `.gitignore`. With sign in or Postgres, it also gets a `.env` with random secrets, which is not committed.

## Build the command

Pick what you want, and copy the command for your system. It skips every question.

To write the command by hand, add `--yes` and any options from the table. Turn something off with `--no-`, such as `--no-lucide`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/main/scripts/setup.sh | sh -s -- --yes --name=shop
```

On Windows, `irm ... | iex` cannot pass options, so run the script as a script block. Put options that contain a comma, such as `--locales=en,de`, in single quotes, or PowerShell splits them:

```powershell
powershell -c "& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/main/scripts/setup.ps1))) --yes --name=shop --i18n '--locales=en,de'"
```

Next, build something real in the [tutorial](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/tutorial).

Prefer to read scripts before running them? They are in [`scripts/`](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/tree/main/scripts).

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/tutorial

# Tutorial: a notes app

Build a small notes app from an empty folder: a Ktor API, a SvelteKit page that calls it through the generated client, validation on both sides, and one JAR at the end. It takes about 20 minutes. The finished, larger version is [`examples/notes`](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/tree/main/examples/notes).

You need Java 17 or newer and one of Bun, pnpm, npm or Yarn.

## 1. Create the project

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/main/scripts/setup.sh | sh -s -- --yes --name=notes --package=notes
cd notes
./gradlew svelteDevAll
```

On Windows, use the PowerShell command from [Getting started](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/getting-started) with the same options. `svelteDevAll` starts Vite, the Kotlin compiler and the app, and opens `http://localhost:8080` once everything answers. Leave it running: every step below reloads on save.

The project has `generateTs = true` in `install(Svelte)`, so the TypeScript client in `frontend/src/lib/api/` is rewritten from your routes each time the app starts.

## 2. Model the notes

Create `src/main/kotlin/Notes.kt` next to `Application.kt`:

```kotlin
package notes

import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Validated
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Validator
import io.ktor.openapi.JsonSchema
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger

@Serializable
enum class NoteStatus { ACTIVE, ARCHIVED }

@Serializable
data class Note(
    val id: Int,
    val title: String,
    val body: String,
    val status: NoteStatus,
)

@Serializable
data class NoteInput(
    @JsonSchema.MinLength(1)
    @JsonSchema.MaxLength(80)
    val title: String,
    val body: String = "",
) : Validated {
    override fun Validator.rules() {
        check(::title, title.isNotBlank()) { "A note needs a title." }
    }
}

class NoteStore {
    private val ids = AtomicInteger()
    private val notes = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, Note>()

    fun list(): List<Note> = notes.values.sortedBy { it.id }

    fun create(input: NoteInput): Note = Note(ids.incrementAndGet(), input.title, input.body, NoteStatus.ACTIVE).also { notes[it.id] = it }

    fun archive(id: Int): Note? = notes.computeIfPresent(id) { _, note -> note.copy(status = NoteStatus.ARCHIVED) }

    fun delete(id: Int): Boolean = notes.remove(id) != null
}
```

The schema annotations and the `Validated` rules do two jobs. ktor-svelte checks every received `NoteInput` against them and answers 422 with field errors, and the generated client gets the same limits for your form.

## 3. Add the routes

Create `src/main/kotlin/NoteRoutes.kt`:

```kotlin
package notes

import io.ktor.http.HttpStatusCode
import io.ktor.server.request.receive
import io.ktor.server.response.respond
import io.ktor.server.routing.Route
import io.ktor.server.routing.delete
import io.ktor.server.routing.get
import io.ktor.server.routing.post
import io.ktor.server.routing.route

fun Route.noteRoutes(store: NoteStore) {
    route("/api/notes") {
        get {
            val notes: List<Note> = store.list()
            call.respond(notes)
        }
        post {
            val input = call.receive<NoteInput>()
            call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, store.create(input))
        }
        post("/{id}/archive") {
            val note: Note? = store.archive(call.parameters["id"]?.toIntOrNull() ?: -1)
            if (note == null) call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound) else call.respond(note)
        }
        delete("/{id}") {
            val deleted = store.delete(call.parameters["id"]?.toIntOrNull() ?: -1)
            call.respond(if (deleted) HttpStatusCode.NoContent else HttpStatusCode.NotFound)
        }
    }
}
```

Register them in `Application.kt`. Create the store above the existing `routing { }` block and add the routes inside it:

```kotlin
val store = NoteStore()
routing {
    noteRoutes(store)
}
```

Save. The app restarts, and `frontend/src/lib/api/` now contains `Note`, `NoteInput`, a `Status` enum and a `notes` service with `list`, `create`, `archive` and `delete`. Enums are named after the property that uses them, so `status: NoteStatus` becomes `Status`. Open `http://localhost:8080/_ktor-svelte/routes` to see your routes next to the frontend pages.

## 4. Load notes into a page

Create `frontend/src/routes/notes/+page.ts`:

```ts
import { apiWith } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const prerender = false;
export const ssr = false;

export const load: PageLoad = async (event) => ({
    notes: await apiWith(event).notes.list()
});
```

The page depends on data from your API, so it is rendered in the browser and not at build time. `apiWith(event)` uses SvelteKit's `fetch` inside `load`.

## 5. Show and change them

Create `frontend/src/routes/notes/+page.svelte`:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, isValidationError, NoteInput, Status, type Note } from '#api';
    import type { PageProps } from './$types';

    let { data }: PageProps = $props();

    let notes = $state<Note[]>([]);
    let title = $state('');
    let body = $state('');
    let errors = $state<Record<string, string[]>>({});

    $effect(() => {
        notes = data.notes;
    });

    async function refresh() {
        notes = await api.notes.list();
    }

    async function create(event: SubmitEvent) {
        event.preventDefault();
        const draft: NoteInput = { title, body };
        errors = NoteInput.validate(draft);
        if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) return;
        try {
            await api.notes.create(draft);
            title = body = '';
            await refresh();
        } catch (error) {
            if (!isValidationError(error)) throw error;
            errors = error.body.fields;
        }
    }
</script>

<h1 class="text-3xl font-bold">Notes</h1>

<form class="my-6 grid gap-2" onsubmit={create}>
    <input class="input w-full" placeholder="Title" bind:value={title} />
    {#each errors.title ?? [] as message}
        <p class="text-error text-sm">{message}</p>
    {/each}
    <textarea class="textarea w-full" placeholder="Body" bind:value={body}></textarea>
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Add note</button>
</form>

<ul class="grid gap-2">
    {#each notes as note (note.id)}
        <li class="card bg-base-200 p-4" class:opacity-60={note.status === Status.ARCHIVED}>
            <strong>{note.title}</strong>
            <p>{note.body}</p>
            <div class="flex gap-2">
                <button class="btn btn-xs" disabled={note.status === Status.ARCHIVED} onclick={() => api.notes.archive(note.id).then(refresh)}>Archive</button>
                <button class="btn btn-xs btn-error" onclick={() => api.notes.delete(note.id).then(refresh)}>Delete</button>
            </div>
        </li>
    {:else}
        <li>No notes yet.</li>
    {/each}
</ul>
```

Open `http://localhost:8080/notes`. Add a note, archive it, delete it. Every call is typed: rename `body` in `NoteInput`, save, and `svelte-check` points at each line that needs to change.

Submit an empty title: `NoteInput.validate` shows "Must be at least 1 character." without sending a request, because the generated client knows the `MinLength` annotation. Now type only spaces: that passes the browser check, but the `isNotBlank` rule runs on the server, which answers 422, and `isValidationError` shows "A note needs a title." under the field.

## 6. Pass config to the frontend

Values that differ per environment, such as the app name, come from Ktor at startup. Add a class to `Notes.kt`:

```kotlin
@Serializable
data class AppConfig(
    val appName: String,
)
```

Pass it in `install(Svelte)`. `env` comes with the generated project and also reads `.env`:

```kotlin
publicConfig(AppConfig(appName = env("APP_NAME") ?: "Notes"))
```

Load it next to the notes in `frontend/src/routes/notes/+page.ts`:

```ts
import { apiWith, loadPublicConfig } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const prerender = false;
export const ssr = false;

export const load: PageLoad = async (event) => ({
    notes: await apiWith(event).notes.list(),
    config: await loadPublicConfig()
});
```

In production the config is inlined into every page, so `loadPublicConfig()` reads it without a request. In development Vite serves the pages, so it is fetched once. Use `{data.config.appName}` as the heading of the page. Never put secrets in it: anyone can read it. See [Runtime config](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config).

## 7. Ship one JAR

Stop `svelteDevAll`, then build and run:

```bash
./gradlew buildFatJar
APP_NAME="My notes" java -jar build/libs/notes-all.jar
```

The JAR contains the API, the built frontend and its manifest. Open `http://localhost:8080/notes`: same app, now with compressed, cached files and a strict Content-Security-Policy. See [Deployment](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment) for Docker and reverse proxies.

## Where to go next

- Tags, search, paging and uploads: [examples/notes](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/tree/main/examples/notes) and the [recipes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes)
- Sign-in with a session cookie: [Sessions](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions)
- Everything the client can do: [Calling the API](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api)

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/existing-project

# Add to an existing project

Already have a Ktor app, a SvelteKit app, or both? Add ktor-svelte in a few steps.

Add the plugin to a Kotlin JVM project that uses the `application` plugin, in `build.gradle.kts`:

<!-- x-release-please-start-version -->
```kotlin
plugins {
    id("io.github.nijasc.ktor-svelte") version "0.10.1"
}
```
<!-- x-release-please-end -->

Create the frontend. This writes a working SvelteKit 3 project to `frontend/`, with a `.gitignore` and an `.editorconfig` that matches the Kotlin side, and installs it with the first package manager on your `PATH`:

```bash
./gradlew svelteInit
```

Already have a frontend? It needs `adapter-static`, and since SvelteKit 3 has no `svelte.config.js`, the configuration goes in `frontend/vite.config.ts`. Run `./gradlew svelteDoctor` to check the rest:

```ts
import { sveltekit } from '@sveltejs/kit/vite';
import adapter from '@sveltejs/adapter-static';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [sveltekit({ adapter: adapter({ fallback: '200.html' }) })],
    server: { hmr: { clientPort: 5173 } }
});
```

Install the Ktor plugin:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Svelte

fun Application.module() {
    install(Svelte)

    routing {
        get("/api/hello") { call.respondText("hi") }
    }
}
```

Run it. The frontend is built first and served from the same port as your API:

```bash
./gradlew run
```

For one runnable JAR, add [Shadow](https://gradleup.com/shadow/) or Ktor's Gradle plugin and run `shadowJar` or `buildFatJar`. The frontend comes along automatically.

Want an IDE setup? This writes run configurations to `.run/`:

```bash
./gradlew svelteGenerateRunConfigurations
```

The Gradle plugin adds the runtime for you. If you only want the library, add it directly:

<!-- x-release-please-start-version -->
```kotlin
implementation("io.github.nijasc:ktor-svelte-server:0.10.1")
```
<!-- x-release-please-end -->

To keep Kotlin, Ktor and ktor-svelte on versions that are tested together, import the published version catalog in `settings.gradle.kts`:

<!-- x-release-please-start-version -->
```kotlin
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    versionCatalogs {
        create("ktorSvelte") {
            from("io.github.nijasc:ktor-svelte-catalog:0.10.1")
        }
    }
}
```
<!-- x-release-please-end -->

Then use its aliases in `build.gradle.kts`, and upgrade everything by changing that one version:

```kotlin
plugins {
    alias(ktorSvelte.plugins.kotlin.jvm)
    alias(ktorSvelte.plugins.kotlin.serialization)
    alias(ktorSvelte.plugins.ktor)
    alias(ktorSvelte.plugins.ktor.svelte)
}

dependencies {
    implementation(ktorSvelte.ktor.server.netty)
}
```

It has the `kotlin`, `ktor`, `serialization` and `ktor-svelte` versions, the plugins above, `ktor-svelte-server`, `ktor-bom`, the common Ktor server modules and `kotlinx-serialization-json`.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/project-structure

# Project structure

A project created by the setup script looks like this. Projects that add ktor-svelte to an existing app have the same core: a Gradle build with the plugin, a Ktor app with `install(Svelte)`, and a SvelteKit app in `frontend/`.

```
my-app/
  build.gradle.kts            plugins, svelte { } settings, dependencies
  settings.gradle.kts
  gradle/libs.versions.toml   version catalog
  src/main/kotlin/
    Application.kt            embeddedServer, install(Svelte), routes
    Env.kt                    typed access to environment variables
    Errors.kt                 typed error responses
  src/main/resources/
    logback.xml
  frontend/
    package.json
    vite.config.ts            generated by ktor-svelte
    vite.user.ts              your own Vite settings
    src/
      app.html
      routes/                 your pages
      lib/api/                generated TypeScript client
      lib/ktor-svelte/        generated helpers for themes, icons and i18n
    messages/                 i18n message files, if i18n is on
  .run/                       IntelliJ run configurations
  .env.example                every variable the app reads
  Dockerfile                  if you chose Docker
```

## Files you own and files ktor-svelte owns

ktor-svelte writes some files for you and keeps them up to date. Each of them starts with a "Generated by ktor-svelte" header. Do not edit them, because the next sync or start overwrites your changes.

| File | Written by | Changes when |
|---|---|---|
| `frontend/src/lib/api/*` | the app in development, or `svelteGenerateTs` | a route or DTO changes |
| `frontend/vite.config.ts` | `svelteSync` | library settings change |
| `frontend/src/lib/ktor-svelte/*` | `svelteSync` | themes, icons or locales change |
| `frontend/src/hooks*.ts` | `svelteSync` | i18n or theme settings change |
| Kotlin `AppTheme` and `Messages` classes | the Gradle build, in `build/generated`, never committed | themes or messages change |

Everything else is yours. ktor-svelte never overwrites a file without the header. If it needs to own a file you already have, such as your own `vite.config.ts`, the build stops and tells you what to move. Put custom Vite settings in `vite.user.ts`.

Commit the generated frontend files. A frontend build never needs the JVM app to run first, and `svelteVerifyTs` and `svelteVerifySync` in `check` fail when they are out of date, so a changed DTO cannot drift away from the frontend unnoticed.

## The `#api` import

`svelteInit` and `svelteSync` add an import alias to `frontend/package.json`, so pages import the generated client the same way wherever they are:

```ts
import { api, isApiError, type Note } from '#api';
```

## What ends up in the JAR

`svelteBundle` copies the static build into `ktor-svelte/public/` in your resources and writes `ktor-svelte/manifest.json`. Hidden files such as `.env` and source maps are left out. The [How it works](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/how-it-works) page explains how requests are answered from the manifest.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow

# Dev workflow

Hot reload for Svelte and Kotlin, debugging and the dev proxy.

One command runs everything. Then open Ktor's port, not Vite's:

```bash
./gradlew svelteDevAll
```

It starts Vite, keeps Kotlin compiling and runs your app. Save a Svelte file and the page hot reloads. Save a Kotlin file and the app restarts, and with `generateTs` on your TypeScript updates a moment later, so type errors show up in the editor right away. A restart loses anything your app keeps in memory. Stopping the task stops all three. In IntelliJ, this is the `Dev` run configuration.

All three write to one console in the same shape, so you can tell them apart at a glance:

```text
10:17:17  app      INFO   Application started in 0.959 seconds.
10:17:17  vite     INFO   (ssr) connected.
10:17:31  kotlin   ERROR  src/main/kotlin/shop/Routes.kt:24:16 Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'String'.
10:17:32  kotlin   ERROR  does not compile: 1 error
10:17:34  kotlin   INFO   compiled
```

Each source has its own color, and warnings and errors stand out. App lines keep the time and level your logging framework printed, and show the logger's class name when it isn't `Application`. Vite's start banner, its copies of browser console messages, which ktor-svelte forwards itself, and Gradle's build failure boilerplate are left out, because the ready message above already lists the URLs and the compiler errors say what failed. Colors are off when `CI` or `NO_COLOR` is set, or the terminal is `dumb`.

When Kotlin stops compiling, the app keeps running its last good version, and the compiler errors appear in the browser in Vite's error overlay, with the file and line of each. Click the file to open it in your editor, or press Esc to hide the overlay until the errors change. It disappears once the code compiles again.

An **API** button in the bottom right corner of the page lists the last 100 API calls the app answered: method, path, status, how long the server took, and the `X-Request-Id` on hover. Calls that failed validation show the message for each field, and the button turns red while any call failed. It only exists while ktor-svelte proxies to Vite, so production pages never contain it. Turn it off with `dev { panel = false }`.

Browser console output lands in the same console as your app. Every `console.log`, `info`, `debug`, `warn` and `error`, uncaught errors and unhandled promise rejections are sent to the app and logged by the `ktor-svelte.browser` logger, with the page they came from:

```text
10:21:19 WARN  ktor-svelte.browser Probe warning {"id":7} [/notes]
10:21:19 ERROR ktor-svelte.browser Error: Probe crash
```

Objects are written as JSON, and errors with their stack trace. `console.debug` uses the DEBUG level, so it only shows when you enable it in your logging configuration. Like the panel, this only exists while ktor-svelte proxies to Vite, and only for requests from this machine. Turn it off with `dev { browserLogs = false }`.

Once the app is listening, it prints the links you need, so they do not get lost in the output:

```
ktor-svelte is ready. Open the app URL, not the Vite one:
  App:      http://localhost:8080
  API docs: http://localhost:8080/api/docs
  Vite:     http://localhost:5173
```

It also opens the app in your default browser, the first time only, so restarts do not open new tabs. It never does so in CI or on a Linux machine without a display. Turn it off with `svelte { dev { openBrowser = false } }`. The API docs line appears when `apiDocs = true`. After a restart it prints one line with the app URL instead. The URL comes from Ktor's `Responding at` log line, so keep Ktor's INFO logging on for the application logger.

For the edits you make most, install the live templates once with `./gradlew svelteLiveTemplates --install` and restart the IDE. In Kotlin, `ksget`, `kspost` and `kspage` write routes, and `ksdto` and `ksinput` write DTOs with bounds and rules. In TypeScript, `ksapi` calls the generated client, `ksload` writes a `load` function with `apiWith`, and `kserror` wraps code in typed error handling.

To debug your Kotlin code, start `Dev` as usual and then start the `Debug app` run configuration in debug mode. IntelliJ debugs Gradle tasks only when they run a JVM through Gradle, and `svelteDevAll` starts the app itself, so the app instead listens for a debugger on `127.0.0.1:5005` (see `dev.debugPort`). `Debug app` has auto restart on, so it reconnects after each restart. Outside IntelliJ, attach any JDWP debugger to that port. Two apps running `svelteDevAll` at once need different debug ports.

At startup in development, the app logs which protections and settings are active, so a 403, 413 or 429 does not come as a surprise:

```
ktor-svelte settings:
  API prefixes: /api
  Dev proxy: http://localhost:5173
  Origin check: on (same host only)
  Body limit: 1 MiB, JSON depth: 64
  Rate limit: 120 writes per 1m per client, FixedWindow
  Content-Security-Policy: off while proxying to Vite
  Error details: hidden in production, shown now
  API compression: on, request IDs: on
```

Production logs only the version and the build fingerprint.

In development, API calls that take 500 ms or longer are logged with the route that served them, so you can jump straight to the code:

```
ktor-svelte: slow API call GET /api/notes?search=milk took 812 ms (notes/Routes.kt:19)
```

Change the threshold with `dev { slowApiCall = 200.milliseconds }`, or set it to `null` to turn it off. Production never logs these.

Open `http://localhost:8080/_ktor-svelte/routes` to see every Ktor route next to every SvelteKit page, with the file and line of each route and a warning on routes that hide a page. Ask for `application/json` to get the same table as JSON. It exists only in development and answers only requests from this machine.

Prefer separate terminals? Run these instead:

```bash
./gradlew svelteDev
```

```bash
./gradlew run -Psvelte.dev=true
```

In development mode the runtime proxies to Vite if it is reachable, otherwise serves built files if they exist, and otherwise returns a 503 explaining how to start Vite. API prefixes are never proxied.

The proxy only answers requests from this machine, so your frontend source is not open to everyone on your network, even though Ktor listens on all interfaces. Requests from elsewhere get your built files, or a 403 if there are none. It never forwards cookies or `Authorization` headers. It also refuses to start if `dev.url` points at another machine. To test from your phone or use Vite in another container, set `dev { allowRemote = true }`, and only on a network you trust.

The proxy forwards HTTP only. POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests are forwarded too, with their body, so Vite endpoints and SvelteKit form actions work in dev. Paths under your API prefixes are never proxied, whatever the method. `server.hmr.clientPort` in the quick start makes Vite's client connect straight to Vite. Without it HMR still works, but the browser logs one WebSocket error before Vite falls back. Either way, the browser must be able to reach Vite's port, so a remote machine or container needs that port exposed.

With two terminals, if a Gradle process is killed rather than stopped normally, Vite or the app can keep running and hold its port. Run `./gradlew --stop`, or stop the process listening on that port. `svelteDevAll` stops its children even when its terminal is closed.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment

# Deployment

A ktor-svelte app is one JVM process. The frontend is inside the JAR, so there is no Node, no second server and no CORS setup in production.

## Build the JAR

Any of Gradle's usual ways to package a Ktor app works, and each one builds the frontend first:

```bash
./gradlew buildFatJar
```

```bash
./gradlew shadowJar
```

```bash
./gradlew installDist
```

`buildFatJar` comes with the Ktor Gradle plugin and `shadowJar` with Shadow. Both write one runnable JAR to `build/libs/`. `installDist` from the `application` plugin writes a folder with start scripts and every dependency as its own JAR.

Run it:

```bash
java -jar build/libs/my-app-all.jar
```

The app starts in production mode unless you pass `-Dio.ktor.development=true`. In production, a missing frontend build stops the app at startup, the dev proxy is off, error details are hidden, and every page gets its Content-Security-Policy.

At startup the app logs which ktor-svelte version and which frontend build it serves:

```
ktor-svelte 0.9.0 serves frontend build b3f58012c3ff with 19 files
```

The fingerprint is a hash of every file in the build, so two servers with the same fingerprint serve exactly the same frontend. The status endpoint reports the full fingerprint.

Keep secrets in environment variables, never in `publicConfig` or the frontend. Projects from the setup script read them in `Env.kt` and list them in `.env.example`.

## Docker

The setup script writes this `Dockerfile` when you choose Docker. It builds the JAR in one stage and runs it as a non-root user in a small JRE image:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
COPY --from=node:24-slim /usr/local/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node
COPY --from=node:24-slim /usr/local/lib/node_modules /usr/local/lib/node_modules
RUN ln -s /usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npm
RUN npm install -g bun
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN chmod +x gradlew && ./gradlew buildFatJar --no-daemon --console=plain
RUN cp build/libs/*-all.jar /app.jar

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system --no-create-home app
COPY --from=build /app.jar /app.jar
USER app
ENV PORT=8080
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

The `RUN npm install -g bun` line installs the package manager the project uses. Keep `node_modules`, `.svelte-kit`, `build` and `.env` out of the image with a `.dockerignore`.

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env my-app
```

## A plain server

Copy the JAR to the server and run it as a service. A minimal systemd unit:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=my-app
After=network.target

[Service]
User=my-app
EnvironmentFile=/etc/my-app.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/my-app/my-app-all.jar
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

## Behind a reverse proxy

Most deployments put nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer or a platform router in front of the app to terminate TLS. Then:

- **Install `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders`** from `ktor-server-forwarded-header`. The rate limit tells clients apart by their address, and without these plugins every user shares the proxy's address and one limit. The origin check also compares hosts through them.
- **Send HSTS from the proxy**, since only the proxy knows about TLS.
- **Do not compress twice.** The app already compresses API responses and serves precompressed files. Let the proxy pass `Content-Encoding` through.
- **Point health checks at the health endpoint.** Turn it on with `healthEndpoint = true`, and check `GET /_ktor-svelte/health`. See [Built-in endpoints](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints).

## Faster responses

- Add `io.ktor:ktor-server-compression-zstd` to serve API responses with zstd to browsers that accept it. It adds a native library of about 7 MB. See [Transport and compression](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/transport).
- Set `adapter({ precompress: true })` in `frontend/vite.config.ts`, or keep `svelte { precompress = true }`, so files are compressed once at build time instead of on every request.
- Hashed files under `_app/immutable/` are cached for a year, so returning visitors only download what changed after a deploy.

## Checklist

- The JAR was built without `-Psvelte.skip=true` or `-Psvelte.dev=true`.
- The app runs without `-Dio.ktor.development=true`.
- Secrets come from the environment.
- `XForwardedHeaders` is installed when a proxy sits in front.
- `GET /_ktor-svelte/health` answers 200 if your platform checks health.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/examples

# Examples

Two example apps live in the repository. They are separate Gradle builds that use ktor-svelte the way your project does, and they double as the end-to-end tests, so they always work with the current code.

## Run them

Clone the repository, then start an example with everything in one command:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte.git
cd ktor-svelte
./gradlew -p examples/notes svelteDevAll
```

Open `http://localhost:8080`. In IntelliJ, open the repository and run the `Notes: Dev` or `Basic: Dev` run configuration instead. You need Java 17 or newer and [Bun](https://bun.sh).

To build and run the production JAR:

```bash
./gradlew -p examples/notes buildFatJar
```

```bash
java -jar examples/notes/build/libs/notes-all.jar
```

## basic

[`examples/basic`](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/tree/main/examples/basic) is the smallest possible app.

| Look at | To see |
|---|---|
| `src/main/kotlin/Application.kt` | `install(Svelte)` with no settings, and one API route |
| `frontend/src/routes/+page.svelte`, `about/` | Prerendered pages |
| `frontend/src/routes/app/` | A page that renders in the browser and calls the API |
| `frontend/vite.config.ts` | The `adapter-static` setup SvelteKit needs |

## notes

[`examples/notes`](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/tree/main/examples/notes) is a small notes app that uses almost every feature.

| Look at | To see |
|---|---|
| `src/main/kotlin/notes/Application.kt` | `generateTs`, `transport { json(); xml(); compression() }`, `publicConfig` and `apiDocs` |
| `src/main/kotlin/notes/Model.kt` | DTOs with `@JsonSchema` bounds and `Validated` rules, `Page<Note>` |
| `src/main/kotlin/notes/Routes.kt` | CRUD routes, typed 404 errors, a paged feed and multipart attachments |
| `frontend/src/lib/api/` | The generated client, committed |
| `frontend/src/routes/notes/+page.svelte` | Forms with `use:field`, client and server validation, search and tag filters |
| `frontend/src/routes/notes/[id]/` | A dynamic route with `apiWith(event)` in `load` and typed errors |
| `frontend/src/routes/+layout.svelte` | DaisyUI themes, Lucide icons and i18n with a language switcher |
| `src/e2eTest/kotlin/NotesAppTest.kt` | How the production JAR is tested end to end |

Things to try while `svelteDevAll` runs:

- Change a Svelte file: the page updates without a reload.
- Add a property to `Note` in `Model.kt`: the app restarts, and `frontend/src/lib/api/types.ts` gains the property a moment later.
- Open `http://localhost:8080/api/docs` for Swagger UI.
- Submit an empty title: the error comes from the generated `validate()` before any request is sent.

## Your own examples

The [recipes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/) show complete solutions for sessions, uploads, live updates, paging and an admin area that you can copy into your app.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript

# Generated TypeScript

Types, services and validation helpers generated from your Ktor routes, with no npm dependencies.

Set `generateTs = true`. Each time the app starts in development mode, it reads your routing tree, builds an OpenAPI document and writes this to `frontend/src/lib/api`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `types.ts` | An interface or union for every schema, an `empty()` factory for every object, `bounds` and `validate()` where the schema has constraints, a `const` object for every enum, and date types |
| `services.ts` | One object per resource, such as `api.notes.list()` |
| `client.ts` | The small `fetch` wrapper, `ApiError` and `apiConfig` |
| `index.ts` | Re-exports all of the above |
| `openapi.json` | The OpenAPI document itself |

To see the output for your own API before installing anything, paste its OpenAPI document into the [generator playground](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/playground).

Commit these files. That way a frontend build never needs your app to run first. Unchanged files are not rewritten, so Vite does not reload for nothing. Nothing is generated in production.

With the `application` plugin, `check` runs `svelteVerifyTs`. It starts your app once, generates the TypeScript in memory and fails if the committed files differ, so a changed DTO or route can't drift away from the frontend unnoticed. Line endings are ignored. It passes when `generateTs` is off. To fix a failure, run `svelteGenerateTs`, or start the app in development mode, and commit the result. To leave it out of `check`, set `svelte.verifyTs=false` in `gradle.properties` or pass `-Psvelte.verifyTs=false`.

Every Kotlin enum with two or more values becomes a `const` object plus a type of the same name, so you can use the values in code and not only in types:

```ts
import { Status } from '#api';

const archived = notes.filter((note) => note.status === Status.ARCHIVED);
```

Enums that appear in several classes with the same values share one generated name. The name comes from the property, such as `status` becoming `Status`. When two different enums would get the same name, the owning class is added in front, such as `NoteStatus`.

Every object type also gets an `empty()` factory, handy as the initial state of a form:

```ts
import { NoteInput } from '#api';

let draft = $state(NoteInput.empty());
```

Every property is filled in, optional ones included: strings become `''`, numbers `0`, booleans `false`, lists `[]`, maps `{}`, nullable properties `null`, enums their first value, and nested objects their own `empty()`. Each call returns a fresh object.

Properties with [validation annotations](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation) also appear under `bounds`, named like the HTML attributes, so you can spread them onto an input:

```svelte
<input bind:value={draft.title} {...NoteInput.bounds.title} />
```

Strings get `minlength`, `maxlength` and `pattern`, numbers get `min` and `max`. A strict bound on an integer moves by one, and on a decimal it is left out, because HTML has no strict bounds. The browser matches `pattern` against the whole value, while the server only looks for a match inside it, so write patterns with `^` and `$` to get the same result in both.

`required: true` is added only where the server would reject an empty field too, so the browser is never stricter than the server: strings with a minimum length of at least 1, and numbers that are required and not nullable, because an empty number input gives `null`. Nullable properties, booleans, lists, objects and enums never get it. A property with only `required` still gets a `bounds` entry.

Every object type that the server checks against annotations, directly or through a nested object or list, also gets `validate()`. It runs the same checks in the browser and returns errors in the same shape as `fields` of a 422, with the same messages and paths such as `lines[1].sku`, plus `Required.` for an empty required number. An empty object means valid. Types without annotations get no `validate()`, just as the server skips them. One error display then covers both instant feedback and the server answer:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, isValidationError, NoteInput } from '#api';

    let draft = $state(NoteInput.empty());
    let errors = $state<Record<string, string[]>>({});

    async function save(event: SubmitEvent) {
        event.preventDefault();
        errors = NoteInput.validate(draft);
        if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) return;
        try {
            await api.notes.create(draft);
        } catch (error) {
            if (!isValidationError(error)) throw error;
            errors = error.body.fields;
        }
    }
</script>

<form onsubmit={save}>
    <input bind:value={draft.title} oninput={() => (errors = NoteInput.validate(draft))} {...NoteInput.bounds.title} />
    {#if errors.title}<p role="alert">{errors.title.join(' ')}</p>{/if}
</form>
```

Rules in `Validated.rules()` and in `validate { }` inside a route only run on the server, so their errors arrive with the 422.

Dates arrive as strings, but not as plain `string`. A `LocalDate` becomes `IsoDate`, a `LocalTime` becomes `IsoTime`, and an `Instant` or `LocalDateTime` becomes `IsoDateTime`, so a date can't be mixed up with ordinary text. Helpers convert them safely:

```ts
import { IsoDate, IsoDateTime } from '#api';

const due = IsoDate.parse(task.due);
const created = IsoDateTime.parse(note.createdAt).toLocaleString();
const input = { due: IsoDate.today(), remindAt: IsoDateTime.now() };
```

`IsoDate.parse` returns local midnight. `new Date('2026-11-10')` would give UTC midnight instead, which shows the previous day west of Greenwich. For an `Instant` use `IsoDateTime.from(date)`, which writes UTC. For a `LocalDateTime` use `IsoDateTime.fromLocal(date)`, which writes no offset. Both share one OpenAPI format, so the type can't tell them apart. The values of `<input type="date">`, `type="time"` and `type="datetime-local"` already have the right shape for `LocalDate`, `LocalTime` and `LocalDateTime`. The helpers are only generated when your API uses a date.

`svelteInit` also sets up the short `#api` import. For a frontend you already have, add it to `frontend/package.json`:

```json
{
  "imports": {
    "#api": "./src/lib/api/index.ts"
  }
}
```

## Documentation in the editor

A `summary` and `description` set in `describe { }` end up as JSDoc on the generated function, so the editor shows them when you hover over a call:

```kotlin
post("/api/notes/{id}/attachments") { /* ... */ }.describe {
    summary = "Uploads files to a note."
    description = "Send the files as multipart form data."
}
```

```ts
/**
 * Uploads files to a note.
 *
 * Send the files as multipart form data.
 */
export const notesAttachments = (id: string | number, body: FormData, options?: RequestOptions) => ...
```

## Sealed classes

A sealed class or interface becomes a union of its subtypes, each with a literal `type` field, so TypeScript narrows it in a `switch`. The generated companion also lists the type names and has an exhaustive `match`: leave out a case and the code does not compile.

```kotlin
@Serializable
sealed interface Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("created")
data class Created(val at: Instant) : Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("archived")
data class Archived(val at: Instant, val title: String) : Activity
```

```ts
import { Activity, api } from '#api';

const lines = (await api.notes.getActivity(id)).map((item) =>
    Activity.match(item, {
        created: (created) => `Created at ${created.at}`,
        archived: (archived) => `Archived "${archived.title}"`
    })
);
```

Use `@SerialName` for short type names. Without it, the type name is the fully qualified class name.

## Getting exact types

Ktor's compiler plugin reads `call.receive<T>()`, `call.respond()` and `call.queryParameters` for you, so plain routes get full types. Add the Ktor Gradle plugin:

```kotlin
plugins {
    id("io.ktor.plugin") version "3.6.1"
}

ktor {
    openApi {
        enabled = true
        codeInferenceEnabled = true
        onlyCommented = false
    }
}
```

Without it, describe routes by hand. A route with no description still gets a service, but it returns `unknown`:

```kotlin
get("/api/todos") { call.respond(todos) }.describe {
    responses {
        HttpStatusCode.OK { schema = jsonSchema<List<Todo>>() }
    }
}
```

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/playground

# Generator playground

Paste an OpenAPI document and see the TypeScript that `generateTs` writes for it. The playground runs the same generator as the Ktor plugin, compiled to JavaScript, so nothing leaves your browser.

Only paths under the API prefix are kept, as in your app. The document must be JSON, which is what Ktor produces. In a real project the generator also adds the `LucideIcon` type when `lucide` is enabled and `readPublicConfig()` when you set `publicConfig`, so those are missing here. See [Generated TypeScript](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript) for what each file contains and how to use it.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api

# Calling the API

Use the generated client from components and load functions, handle typed errors, stream events, page through lists and upload files.

```ts
import { api, apiConfig } from '#api';

const notes = await api.notes.list({ search: 'milk' });
const note = await api.notes.get(1);
await api.notes.update(1, { title: 'Oat milk' });

apiConfig.headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer token';
```

When several components load the same data at the same time, set `apiConfig.dedupeGets = true`. Identical GET requests that are still in flight then share one network request and get the same parsed result, so do not mutate it. Calls with their own `headers`, `fetch` or `signal` are never shared, and nothing is cached after a response arrives. It is off by default.

## Prefetch on hover

Projects created by ktor-svelte set `data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover"` on `<body>`, so SvelteKit runs a page's `load` function when the pointer rests on a link to it. A `load` that calls the API through `apiWith(event)` therefore fetches its data before the click, and the page opens without waiting. Add the attribute to `src/app.html` in older projects.

For data a component fetches itself, prefetch the call. The next identical GET within 10 seconds gets that response instead of a new request, once:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, prefetchOnHover } from '#api';
</script>

{#each notes as note (note.id)}
    <a href="/notes/{note.id}" use:prefetchOnHover={() => api.notes.get(note.id)}>{note.title}</a>
{/each}
```

`prefetchOnHover` starts after the pointer rests for 50 ms, or at once on focus or touch. Call `prefetch(() => api.notes.get(id))` yourself for other triggers, and pass a second argument to change how long the result is kept, in milliseconds. Only GET requests made synchronously inside the callback are prefetched, without their own `headers` or `signal`, and a failed prefetch is simply forgotten.

Errors are typed too. Ktor's compiler plugin finds error responses such as `call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem(...))`, and `isApiError` narrows the body:

```ts
import { api, isApiError, isValidationError } from '#api';

try {
    await api.notes.create({ title: '' });
} catch (error) {
    if (isValidationError(error)) showErrors(error.body.fields);
    if (isApiError(error, 'notes.get')) console.log(error.body.message);
}
```

Errors that `StatusPages` sends are invisible to the compiler plugin, because its handlers are plain lambdas. Declare them once, and they join the typed errors of every API endpoint, unless a route already declares that status itself:

```kotlin
install(StatusPages) {
    exception<NotFoundException> { call, cause -> call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem(cause.message.orEmpty())) }
}
install(Svelte) {
    errorResponse<Problem>(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}
```

Routes that declare a `text/event-stream` response, for example through `describe`, become async generators. Each event's `data` is parsed as JSON when possible, and the stream ends when the connection closes or you stop iterating:

```ts
for await (const tick of api.ticks.watch()) console.log(tick);
```

Every endpoint is also exported on its own, named after its group and service, such as `notesList` or `notesGet`. Import those in pages that use only a few endpoints, and the bundler leaves the rest of the client out of that page:

```ts
import { notesGet } from '#api';

const note = await notesGet(1);
```

For paged lists, return `Page<T>` from `io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte` and read a `cursor` query parameter. `next` is the cursor of the following page, or `null` on the last one:

```kotlin
get("/api/notes/feed") {
    val cursor = call.queryParameters["cursor"]
    val page: Page<Note> = store.page(cursor, limit = 20)
    call.respond(page)
}
```

`pages` turns any such endpoint into an async iterator that fetches one page at a time, typed from the endpoint:

```ts
import { api, pages } from '#api';

for await (const notes of pages(api.notes.getFeed, { limit: '50' })) render(notes);
```

Uploads work with `FormData`. Ktor cannot infer a multipart body from `receiveMultipart`, so describe it once, and the generated function takes `body: FormData`:

```kotlin
post("/api/notes/{id}/attachments") {
    call.receiveMultipart().forEachPart { part -> part.dispose() }
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)
}.describe {
    requestBody { ContentType.MultiPart.FormData() }
}
```

Pass `onUploadProgress` to follow the upload. `fetch` cannot report upload progress, so such a call uses `XMLHttpRequest` instead, with the same headers, errors and `signal` support:

```ts
const form = new FormData();
form.append('file', file);
await api.notes.attachments(id, form, {
    onUploadProgress: ({ loaded, total }) => (progress = total ? loaded / total : 0)
});
```

Uploads count towards `maxApiBodySize`, which is 1 MiB by default, so raise it for routes that accept files.

Service names follow your routes: `GET /notes` is `list`, `GET /notes/{id}` is `get`, `POST` is `create`, `PUT` is `update`, `DELETE` is `delete`, and `POST /notes/{id}/archive` is `archive`. Set `operationId` in `describe` to choose your own. Inside a SvelteKit `load`, use `apiWith(event)`. It is the same client, but every call goes through SvelteKit's `fetch`, which prerendering and client-side navigation need:

```ts
import { apiWith } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const load: PageLoad = async (event) => {
    const api = apiWith(event);
    return { notes: await api.notes.list(), stats: await api.stats.list() };
};
```

In development, ktor-svelte also writes `build/ktor-svelte/routes.json`, which maps every generated service to the Kotlin route that serves it:

```json
"notes.get": { "method": "GET", "path": "/api/notes/{id}", "file": "notes/Routes.kt", "line": 43 }
```

Search it for the operation name you see in the frontend, or let an editor plugin use it to jump from a call to its route. `file` is relative to your source root, and `line` is the line of the route's handler. It lives in `build/` because line numbers change with every edit. When ktor-svelte cannot read a handler's location, the entry has only `method` and `path`.

A `fetch` passed in the options of a single call still wins.

To refresh the files without your dev server, for example in CI, run the task below and check for a diff. It starts your app once, so the app's port must be free.

```bash
./gradlew svelteGenerateTs
```

## Reload after a deploy

Every API response carries the fingerprint of the frontend build the server runs, in the `X-Ktor-Svelte-Build` header. When a response reports a different build than the first one the page saw, the client calls `apiConfig.onNewBuild`, so you can offer a reload instead of running old code against a new API:

```ts
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.onNewBuild = () => {
    showToast('A new version is available.', { action: 'Reload', onAction: () => location.reload() });
};
```

Set `buildHeader = false` in `install(Svelte)` to leave the header out.

## Request IDs

Every call from the generated client sends a fresh `X-Request-Id`. The server keeps it when it is well formed, letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores up to 128 characters, or generates one, and sends it back in the response. Unhandled errors are logged with it, and `ApiError.requestId` carries it, so a user can quote one ID that support finds in the logs:

```ts
try {
    await api.notes.create(draft);
} catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ApiError) showError(`Something went wrong. Reference: ${error.requestId}`);
}
```

The ID is available in routes as `call.callId`, and with Ktor's `CallLogging` you can put it into every log line with `callIdMdc("requestId")`. The client only sends the header to its own origin, so it never causes CORS preflights. If you install Ktor's `CallId` yourself, your setup is used. `requestIds = false` turns it off.

## Timeouts

A request that hangs blocks the UI until the browser gives up, which can take minutes. Set a timeout for every call, or for one:

```ts
import { api, apiConfig, isTimeoutError } from '#api';

apiConfig.timeout = 10_000;

try {
    const report = await api.reports.create(input, { timeout: 60_000 });
} catch (error) {
    if (isTimeoutError(error)) showError('The server took too long. Please try again.');
}
```

A per-call `timeout` wins over `apiConfig.timeout`, and your own `signal` still works next to it. Event streams ignore `apiConfig.timeout`, because a live stream is supposed to stay open. Give one its own `timeout` if you want that.

## Search as you type

When every keystroke starts a request, an older, slower response can arrive after a newer one and overwrite it. Wrap the call in `latest`, and each call aborts the one before it:

```ts
import { api, isAbortError, latest } from '#api';

const search = latest(api.notes.list);

async function onInput(term: string) {
    try {
        notes = await search({ search: term });
    } catch (error) {
        if (!isAbortError(error)) throw error;
    }
}
```

A superseded call always rejects with an `AbortError`, even when it was cancelled while its body was being read. Your own `signal` still works alongside it.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation

# Validation

One set of rules for the server and the browser, with errors per field.

Put simple bounds on the properties with Ktor's `JsonSchema` annotations, and any other rule on the class itself by implementing `Validated`. Both run on every `call.receive` of that class, in every route, for nested classes, lists, map values and sealed subtypes too. Receiving a `List` or `Map` of such classes checks every item. When something fails, the route never runs, and the client gets a 422 with an error list per field, in one standard shape that `isValidationError` understands.

```kotlin
import io.ktor.openapi.JsonSchema

@Serializable
data class NoteInput(
    @JsonSchema.MaxLength(80)
    val title: String,
    val body: String = "",
) : Validated {
    override fun Validator.rules() {
        check(::title, title.isNotBlank()) { "A note needs a title." }
    }
}

post("/api/notes") {
    val input = call.receive<NoteInput>()
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, store.create(input))
}
```

```json
{ "message": "Validation failed", "fields": { "title": ["A note needs a title."] } }
```

| Annotation | Checks | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `@JsonSchema.MinLength(n)`, `@JsonSchema.MaxLength(n)` | Length of a string | `Must be at most 80 characters.` |
| `@JsonSchema.Minimum(x)`, `@JsonSchema.Maximum(x)` | A number, `exclusive = true` for a strict bound | `Must be at least 1.` |
| `@JsonSchema.Pattern(regex)` | A string contains a match | `Must match ^[a-z]+$.` |

Errors use the JSON name, with paths such as `lines[1].sku` for nested values, `prices[eur].amount` for map values and `[0].sku` for the items of a received list. `check(::title, ...)` names the field from the property, so renaming it in the IDE keeps the error in sync. If the property has a different `@SerialName`, pass the name as a string instead.

With `generateTs`, the same annotations end up in OpenAPI and in the generated TypeScript, so a form gets the bounds without asking the server, and `validate()` checks a value in the browser with the same messages the server sends. See [Generated TypeScript](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#generated-typescript).

For a rule that depends on the route, such as comparing against a database, call `validate { check(...) { ... } }` inside the route. It answers the same way. If you use Ktor's `StatusPages` with a handler for all exceptions, it runs first, so let `ValidationException` through.

`use:field` puts the bounds on an input and shows its errors right after it, with `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` set for screen readers. Pass the same errors whether they come from `validate()` or from a 422:

```svelte
<input bind:value={draft.title} use:field={{ bounds: NoteInput.bounds.title, errors: errors.title, errorClass: 'text-error' }} />
```

The message is a `<p role="alert">` with the class `field-error` unless you pass `errorClass`, and it disappears when the errors are empty.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/transport

# Transport and compression

JSON, XML and other formats, and compressed API responses.

Choose how your API talks inside `install(Svelte)`. Without a `transport` block, nothing is installed and you stay in control.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    transport {
        json { prettyPrint = true }
        xml()
        compression()
    }
}
```

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| `json()` | Adds JSON to Ktor's `ContentNegotiation`. Takes a `kotlinx.serialization` `Json` builder |
| `xml()` | Adds XML. Needs `implementation("io.ktor:ktor-serialization-kotlinx-xml")` in your build |
| `negotiation { }` | Registers any other format, such as CBOR, on `ContentNegotiation` directly |
| `compression { }` | Installs Ktor's `Compression`. Takes its normal configuration, and defaults to gzip and deflate |

The client picks a format with its `Accept` header, and the first format you list is the default. Already installing these plugins yourself? You will get a clear error at startup, so remove one of the two. Files precompressed by your adapter are left alone. The generated TypeScript client always speaks JSON.

## API compression

API responses are compressed by default, without any `transport` block. Responses of 1 KiB or more on your API paths with a JSON, XML, CBOR or text content type are sent with gzip or deflate, whichever the client prefers. Browsers decompress them natively, so the generated client and DevTools see plain JSON, and clients that send no `Accept-Encoding`, such as curl, get plain JSON too. Server-sent events, small responses, other content types and frontend files are left alone, and request bodies are never decompressed.

Add Ktor's zstd module, and current browsers get zstd instead, which compresses about as well as gzip at a fraction of the CPU time:

```kotlin
implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-compression-zstd:<ktor version>")
```

It adds a native library of about 7 MB to your JAR, which is why it is not included by default.

Compression and secrets: a response that contains a secret, such as an API key, next to text an attacker can choose can leak that secret byte by byte through its compressed size (the BREACH attack). ktor-svelte's own CSRF protection uses no tokens, so it is not affected. If one of your endpoints returns such a mix, turn `apiCompression` off or install `Compression` yourself with a condition that skips that route.

If you install `Compression` yourself, before or after `install(Svelte)`, or use `transport { compression() }`, your configuration is used instead. To send API responses uncompressed:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    apiCompression = false
}
```

Why compression and not a binary format: for 5000 notes, gzip cut the time from server to parsed data from 318 ms to 152 ms on a 50 Mbit connection and from 1537 ms to 381 ms on 4G, and zstd to 84 ms and 345 ms. CBOR was 7 percent smaller than JSON before compression and larger after it, and decoding it in JavaScript took about seven times as long as `JSON.parse`, so it never came out ahead.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth

# Auth

Use Ktor authentication with the generated client.

To put the frontend behind Ktor's authentication, take over its routing. List what stays public. Those paths must include your login page and `/_app/*`, or the login page cannot load. Anyone can still download the JS bundles under `/_app`, so keep secrets on the server.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    routing = SvelteRouting.Manual
}

routing {
    svelte(public = listOf("/login", "/_app/*"))
    authenticate("session") {
        svelte()
    }
}
```

Pages served by a plain `svelte()` get `private` caching, so shared proxies do not keep them. Paths in the `public` list keep normal caching.

In the browser, react to expired sessions in one place:

```ts
apiConfig.onUnauthorized = () => goto('/login');
```

In development mode, `svelte(public = ...)` also opens the paths Vite needs, so hot reload works on your login page.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config

# Runtime config

Pass values to the frontend at startup, so one JAR works in every environment. The type comes along with `generateTs`:

```kotlin
@Serializable
data class AppConfig(val sentryDsn: String?)

install(Svelte) {
    publicConfig(AppConfig(sentryDsn = System.getenv("SENTRY_DSN")))
}
```

```ts
import { loadPublicConfig } from '#api';

const config = await loadPublicConfig();
```

The config is also inlined into every page as `<script type="application/json" id="ktor-svelte-config">`, so it is there before your code runs, without a request. Read it synchronously, for example in a store or a component's script:

```ts
import { readPublicConfig } from '#api';

const config = readPublicConfig();
```

`loadPublicConfig()` uses the inlined copy when it is there and only asks the server otherwise, which is the case during development with Vite. The JSON is escaped, so a value cannot close the script tag. Pages with the config are prepared once and cached, with their own ETag and a gzip copy. Set `inlinePublicConfig = false` to keep the config out of pages.

## Changing values without a restart

Pass a function instead of a value when the config comes from somewhere you edit while the app runs, such as a file:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    publicConfig { Json.decodeFromString<AppConfig>(Path("config/public.json").readText()) }
}
```

In development the function runs on every request for the config and for every page, so a saved change shows up on the next page load. Inlined pages get a new ETag when the config changes, so the browser does not keep a stale copy. In production the function runs once at startup and the result is kept, so a broken file fails the start instead of a request.

## Keep secrets out

It is served as JSON from `/_ktor-svelte/config.json` to anyone who asks, so **never put secrets in it**. In SvelteKit, call `loadPublicConfig` only in the browser, because prerendering has no server to ask.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints

# Built-in endpoints

The status and health endpoints and Swagger UI, all off by default.

## Sitemap and robots.txt

Search engines find your pages through `/sitemap.xml` and read `/robots.txt` first. ktor-svelte serves both for you when your build has neither:

- `/sitemap.xml` lists every prerendered page in the build, so `about.html` becomes `/about` and `docs/index.html` becomes `/docs/`. The SPA fallback and the 404 page are left out.
- `/robots.txt` lets crawlers read all pages, keeps them out of your API prefixes and `/_ktor-svelte/`, and points to the sitemap.

Pages that only exist at runtime, such as `/notes/42`, can't be listed, because there is no file for them. URLs in both files must be absolute, so set the public address of your site. Otherwise it is taken from the request, which behind a proxy needs Ktor's `ForwardedHeaders` or `XForwardedHeaders` plugin:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    siteUrl = "https://example.com"
}
```

To write your own, put `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt` in `frontend/static/`. Files from the build always win. `sitemap = false` turns both off. With `routing = SvelteRouting.Manual`, they are only served where you route `svelte()`.

## Default favicon

Browsers ask every site for `/favicon.ico`. Until your app has its own icon, ktor-svelte answers with a ktor-svelte one, so tabs and bookmarks show something and the log has no 404s for it. It serves `/favicon.ico`, `/favicon.svg`, `/favicon.png` and `/apple-touch-icon.png`, cached for a day.

As soon as your build has any of `favicon.ico`, `favicon.svg` or `favicon.png`, for example in `frontend/static/`, none of the defaults are served and yours are used. In development, ktor-svelte checks `frontend/static/` instead. Turn the default off with `defaultFavicon = false`.

## Status endpoint

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    statusEndpoint = true
}
```

`GET /_ktor-svelte/status` returns JSON with the bundled build (`present`, `formatVersion`, `files`, `fingerprint`) and the dev proxy (`proxy`, and when active `url` and `reachable`), and how many requests the security guards refused (`refusals`: `crossOrigin`, `bodyTooLarge`, `rateLimit`). It is off by default, never cached, hidden from the OpenAPI document, and answers only requests from this machine with a local `Host`. Everything else gets 403.

## Health endpoint

For load balancers, container orchestrators and uptime checks:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    healthEndpoint = true
    healthCheck { database.isReachable() }
}
```

`GET /_ktor-svelte/health` answers `200` with `{"status":"up"}` when the frontend can be served and every `healthCheck` returns `true`, and `503` with `{"status":"down"}` otherwise. A check that throws counts as down and is logged. Unlike the status endpoint, it answers every client, because it reveals nothing beyond up or down. It is off by default, never cached and hidden from the OpenAPI document.

## API docs

`apiDocs = true` serves Swagger UI at `/api/docs` in development mode only, using the same OpenAPI document as `generateTs`. Change the path with `apiDocsPath`. The page loads its scripts from a public CDN, so it needs internet access.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries

# Frontend libraries

Tailwind, DaisyUI, Lucide, i18n and image optimization, configured in Gradle with typed helpers on both sides.

Turn on what you need in `build.gradle.kts`. Packages get installed and configured for you, and everything works together, including across Kotlin and TypeScript.

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.gradle.DaisyTheme
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.gradle.LocaleStrategy

svelte {
    libraries {
        tailwind {
            typography()
            forms()
        }
        daisyUi {
            themes(DaisyTheme.Light, DaisyTheme.Dark, DaisyTheme.Cupcake)
            customTheme("brand") {
                primary = "#6b57ff"
                base100 = "#fdfcff"
            }
            defaultTheme(DaisyTheme.Light)
            prefersDark(DaisyTheme.Dark)
        }
        lucide()
        images()
        i18n {
            locales("en", "de")
            defaultLocale = "en"
            strategy = LocaleStrategy.Cookie
        }
    }
}
```

Then apply it:

```bash
./gradlew svelteSync
```

`svelteSync` adds the packages, updates your lockfile and writes the generated files. Commit the result. `svelteDev` and `svelteDevAll` sync automatically. A production build never changes anything: it fails and asks you to run `svelteSync` if something is out of date.

**ktor-svelte owns `vite.config.ts`** once any library is on. Put your own Vite settings in `vite.user.ts`, and they are merged in:

```ts
export default {
    server: { port: 3000 }
};
```

It also generates `src/hooks.server.ts`, and `src/hooks.ts` for URL prefixes. If you already have your own versions of these files, sync stops rather than overwriting them. It tells you to move your settings and delete the file. To combine your own `handle` with ours, use `sequence` from `@sveltejs/kit/hooks` with `ktorSvelteHandle` from `#lib/ktor-svelte/server-hooks.js`, after removing the generated hook file and any use of a library that needs it.

If you already have `src/routes/+layout.svelte`, add this line once. Without a layout, one is created for you.

```ts
import '#lib/ktor-svelte/app.css';
```

Generated Kotlin lands in the `io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte` package. Change it with `generatedPackage = "com.example.ui"`.

## Tailwind

`tailwind()` installs Tailwind 4 and wires Vite and the CSS. `typography()` and `forms()` add the official plugins. Everything else is normal Tailwind CSS.

## DaisyUI

`daisyUi()` turns on Tailwind as well. With no themes listed, you get `Light` and `Dark`. Themes are typed on both sides, and the saved choice is applied before the first paint, so there is no flash of the wrong theme.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { setTheme, themes } from '#theme';
</script>

{#each themes as theme}
    <button class="btn" onclick={() => setTheme(theme)}>{theme}</button>
{/each}
```

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.AppTheme
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.theme

get("/api/report") {
    val isDark = call.theme == AppTheme.Dark
}
```

`customTheme` also accepts `secondary`, `accent`, `neutral`, `base200`, `base300`, `baseContent`, `info`, `success`, `warning` and `error`, plus `variable("radius-box", "1rem")` for anything else Daisy supports. Pass `colorScheme = "dark"` for dark themes.

The saved theme is applied by a small inline script. The automatic [Content-Security-Policy](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/security#security-headers) allows it by its hash. If you set your own `contentSecurityPolicy`, allow it with SvelteKit's `csp` option in `hash` mode.

## Lucide

`lucide()` generates a `LucideIcon` enum from the installed version, so a misspelled icon is a compile error. Use it in your DTOs and it reaches the frontend as the same type:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.LucideIcon

@Serializable
data class Note(val title: String, val icon: LucideIcon)
```

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import Icon from '#icon';
</script>

<Icon name="ArrowRight" size={20} />
<Icon name={note.icon} class="text-primary" />
```

Each icon loads on demand, so you only download the ones a page uses. An icon's enum name is its Lucide name in PascalCase, such as `arrow-right` to `ArrowRight`. Names starting with a digit get an `Icon` prefix. A misspelled icon name from a client gets a 400 from Ktor.

## Images

`images()` adds SvelteKit's [`@sveltejs/enhanced-img`](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/images#sveltejs-enhanced-img). Keep pictures next to your code, for example in `frontend/src/lib/assets`, and use `enhanced:img` instead of `img`:

```svelte
<enhanced:img src="#lib/assets/hero.png" alt="Our team" sizes="(min-width: 768px) 65ch, 100vw" />
```

At build time, every image becomes AVIF and WebP in several widths, plus a fallback in the original format, inside a `<picture>` with `srcset`, `width` and `height`. Browsers download only the size and format they need, and the layout doesn't jump while the image loads. In the notes example, a 339 KB PNG becomes an 8 KB AVIF for a laptop screen. The files land in `_app/immutable/`, so browsers cache them for a year like any other hashed asset.

Files in `frontend/static/` are copied as they are, because nothing in the build knows where they are used. Move images there to `src/lib/assets` to have them optimized. Processing uses `sharp`, which comes with prebuilt binaries for Windows, macOS and Linux. The first build with many large images takes longer, and later builds reuse Vite's cache.

## i18n

Keep one JSON file per language in `frontend/messages`. Change the folder with `messagesDir`. Files are flat, and `{name}` is a parameter:

```json
{
  "server-greeting": "Hello {name}, greetings from Ktor!",
  "app-title": "Notes"
}
```

Both sides get typed functions from the same files. A missing key or a mismatched parameter in any language fails the build, so translations can't drift.

While `svelteDevAll` or `svelteDev` runs, saving a message file updates the frontend functions at once, and Vite reloads them, with no Gradle run. Under `svelteDevAll` the Kotlin `Messages` follow and the app restarts. With `svelteDev` alone, they update the next time Kotlin compiles. A file with a missing key or a mismatched parameter is reported in the console, and the last good version stays until you fix it.

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { getLocale, localizeHref, locales, m, setLocale } from '#i18n';
</script>

<h1>{m.appTitle()}</h1>
<p>{m.serverGreeting({ name: 'Ada' })}</p>
<a href={localizeHref('/about')}>About</a>
<button onclick={() => setLocale('de')}>Deutsch</button>
```

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.Messages
import io.github.nijasc.ktorsvelte.messages

get("/api/hello") {
    call.respondText(call.messages.serverGreeting("Ada"))
}

val german = Messages.forLocale("de").appTitle()
```

Choose how the language is picked with `strategy`:
